$about: Machine-side knob for the performance gate. The real floor for each
scenario lives in tests/scenarios/<name>.json under expects.
min_ticks_per_second, so a scenario can never drift away from the
performance contract it was written to hold.
floor_multiplier scales every floor at once — set it below 1.0 on a slow
CI box rather than weakening the scenarios themselves.
overrides pins one scenario to an absolute floor, before the multiplier.
$measured_baseline: IT IS LEFT AT 1.0 DELIBERATELY, AND THE GATE IS RED BECAUSE OF IT. Read
this before anyone reaches for the knob.
The perf stage is red on this Linux container for both scenarios. It is
NOT a regression from the seven-builder wave. A/B, measured by the
integrator alone on a quiet box (0 other Godot processes, verified before
and after every reading), three readings each:
scenario      pre-wave afb031b   this tree (11 readings)     floor
Within one sitting the spread is 2-4% on stress_1000 and 2-8% on smoke.
Across sittings smoke wanders further — 263 to 292 — so read its median,
never a single number; that is what tools/perf.sh --repeat is for.
The floors were met when they were set — the record says stress_1000 went
36 -> 122..144 ticks/s and the floor was raised 35 -> 100 on the strength
of it. This box does 75 before a single line of the wave landed. So the
gap between 75 and 100 is the machine, and the ~3% between 76 and 74 is
the wave. Both numbers are in the same column and only one of them is a
regression anybody can fix by writing code.
Lowering floor_multiplier here would turn the stage green in one line and
would also hide the next real regression, because a 25% cushion is wider
than most regressions worth catching. The honest options are to run the
gate on the machine the floors describe, or to re-derive the floors on the
machine that will run it, with the readings above as the starting point.
That is a decision about what this build promises, so it is Maximilian's
and not the integrator's.

The conclusion of the A/B above is unchanged and is not re-litigated here:

THREE THINGS THAT ARE NEW AND ARE WORTH KEEPING.
1. SMOKE'S SPREAD IS WIDER THAN RECORDED, WITHIN ONE SITTING. The note above
says smoke wanders 2-8% inside a sitting and further across them. One
run of five readings on an idle box: 264 · 268 · 272 · 289 · 295 — a 12%
spread with no code change between readings. A single smoke number is
worth even less than the note already says. stress_1000 by contrast is
tight: 4% across five, 1% across three. Read smoke at --repeat=5 or not
at all.
2. 477 CONCURRENT HOSTILES COST NOTHING MEASURABLE, which is the question
[E1] left open and could not answer while four agents shared the box.
tests/combat/stress_1000_night.json — the SAME 1000-structure city as
stress_1000, with three composed assaults on it — ran 7000 ticks in
90.4 / 89.5 / 88.3 s alone: 77.4 · 78.2 · 79.3 ticks/s, 0 errors, peak
combat.enemies_alive 477. That is FASTER per tick than stress_1000's
74-75 on the same city with no combat in it at all, because the ~1000
structure build cost is a fixed charge amortised over 7000 ticks instead
of 3000. The combat and threat work in this wave is not what is holding
these floors down.
3. THAT FIXTURE IS RUN BY NOTHING. It lives in tests/combat/ rather than
tests/scenarios/, so tools/perf.sh --all does not see it, the gate does
not run it, and tests/p00/test_scenarios.gd does not validate it against
_schema.json. It is reachable only by hand, with
--scenario=res://tests/combat/stress_1000_night.json. Its declared floor
of 15 ticks/s is ~5x below what it actually measures, and [E1] says in
the fixture's own description that the slack is deliberate because a
threshold set by the part being measured is not a gate. Both halves of
that are fine; the part nobody decided is that the fixture is now the
only combat-at-scale measurement in the build and no automated stage
reads it. Moving it into tests/scenarios/ makes it a gate; leaving it
where it is makes it a thing an integrator has to remember. That is a
decision about what the build promises, so it is not the integrator's.
tests/feel/feel_perf.tscn, which the note above records failing 3 of 3 on
its WORST SINGLE FRAME: it PASSED 6 of 6 in this wave's gate run on a quiet
box. Same story, same shape — that stage is measuring how busy the machine
is, not what the code does.
